body:
Urban Water Management

A city needs water for drinking, cooking, sanitation, public services, commerce and industry. Sustainable management must consider both the quantity of available water and its quality.

Urban water conservation begins by avoiding unnecessary consumption and reducing losses. Leaking supply pipes, inefficient fixtures and poorly managed distribution systems can waste treated water before it reaches useful purposes.

Rainwater Harvesting and Groundwater Recharge

Rainwater harvesting means collecting and storing rainfall for suitable uses or directing it to an appropriate recharge system. It can reduce dependence on other sources, but its effectiveness depends on rainfall, storage capacity, water quality and site conditions.

Groundwater recharge is not simply the discharge of any water into the soil. Contaminated runoff can harm groundwater; recharge systems require suitable locations and safeguards.

Sewage Treatment and Water Reuse

Water used by households and other establishments becomes wastewater. Untreated sewage may contain disease-causing organisms, organic matter and other pollutants. Discharging it into rivers or lakes can damage water quality and public health.

A sewage treatment plant (STP) removes pollutants through suitable treatment stages. Treated water can then be reused for an appropriate purpose, such as certain industrial processes, landscaping or other non-potable uses, provided the required quality standards are met.

Water suitable for industrial cooling is not automatically safe for drinking. Potable reuse requires much stricter treatment, monitoring and regulatory safeguards.

Stormwater drainage and sewage collection also perform different functions. Stormwater systems carry rainfall runoff, whereas sewerage systems collect wastewater. Poor separation or maintenance can contribute to overflows and pollution.

Gujarat Example: Treated Wastewater for Industry in Surat

On 11 November 2020, Surat Municipal Corporation inaugurated the supply of tertiary-treated wastewater from its Bamroli treatment facility to industrial units associated with the Sachin Textile Process Industries Welfare Association in Sachin GIDC.

Tertiary treatment is an additional treatment stage used to improve water quality beyond earlier treatment stages. The Surat example demonstrates how appropriately treated municipal wastewater can serve industrial demand and substitute for some freshwater use.

Solid Waste Management

Urban solid waste includes discarded food, paper, plastics, glass, metals and other materials from households and establishments. If mixed waste is dumped or burned indiscriminately, it can pollute air, land and water and create health risks.

Sound management begins with waste reduction and segregation at source. Separating waste when it is generated makes safe treatment and material recovery easier.

India's Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026

The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change notified the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 on 27 January 2026. They came into force on 1 April 2026, superseding the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016. These are the rules in force at the selected content cutoff of 2 November 2026.

The 2026 Rules prescribe 4-stream segregation at source:

  • Wet waste: kitchen scraps, vegetable peels and similar biodegradable material. Suitable processing includes composting and biomethanation.
  • Dry waste: paper, plastic, metal, glass and similar materials. These can be sorted at material recovery facilities and suitable fractions sent for recycling.
  • Sanitary waste: used diapers, sanitary towels and similar material requiring secure wrapping and separate handling.
  • Special-care waste: items such as discarded paint containers, bulbs, mercury thermometers and expired medicines, requiring collection through designated or authorised channels.

A material recovery facility (MRF) separates and prepares suitable waste materials for recovery or recycling. Composting biologically decomposes suitable organic matter into a useful soil amendment. Biomethanation uses microorganisms under oxygen-free conditions to produce biogas from suitable organic material.

Landfills remain necessary for some residual waste, but disposing of recoverable materials without separation wastes resources and increases landfill demand.

Urban local bodies organise municipal waste services. State Pollution Control Boards, including the Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB), undertake pollution-control functions within the applicable legal framework. The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) performs national-level pollution-control and guidance functions.

Waste management is not the same as waste prevention. Recycling and treatment manage waste that has already arisen. Avoiding unnecessary waste generation reduces the problem at its source.

Prelims focus

  • Rainwater harvesting concerns collection and suitable use or recharge of rainfall.
  • An STP treats sewage; an MRF sorts materials for recovery.
  • The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 were notified on 27 January 2026 and came into force on 1 April 2026.
  • The 2026 Rules prescribe wet, dry, sanitary and special-care streams.
  • Surat's Bamroli–Sachin example concerns tertiary-treated wastewater supplied for industrial use.
  • Trap: Treated wastewater is not automatically potable, and all dry waste is not necessarily recyclable.

[Sources: NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, Chapter 12, Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems, printed pp. 135–139; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 16, Environmental Issues, sections 16.2 and 16.3; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, notification dated 27 January 2026 and commencement clause; Press Information Bureau, release dated 28 January 2026 on 4-stream segregation; CPCB, Centralised Solid Waste Management Portal, consulted 2 November 2026; Surat Municipal Corporation, City History, entry dated 11 November 2020, consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Sustainable Urban Water, Sanitation and Solid Waste Management

body:
Industry as a System of Inputs and Outputs

Industries transform raw materials into useful goods. Their operations generally require inputs such as materials, water, energy, labour and equipment. Alongside the desired product, production may generate wastewater, solid residues, air emissions or waste heat.

For example, a textile dyeing unit requires fabric, dyes, chemicals, water and energy. If these inputs are poorly managed, more material may be wasted and larger amounts of polluted wastewater may require treatment.

The environmental challenge is therefore not only to dispose of industrial waste safely but also to avoid generating unnecessary waste in the first place.

Meaning of Cleaner Production

Cleaner production is the continuous application of a preventive environmental approach to production processes, products and services to improve efficiency and reduce risks to people and the environment.

The defining feature is prevention at source. A factory examines how materials and energy are used and modifies practices or processes to reduce pollution and waste before they arise.

The United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) uses the related term Resource Efficient and Cleaner Production (RECP). It connects efficient resource use with pollution prevention and improved environmental and social performance.

Practical Methods of Cleaner Production

Good Housekeeping and Maintenance

Simple operational improvements can prevent avoidable losses. Examples include repairing leaking valves, maintaining machinery, preventing chemical spills, measuring water use and keeping materials in suitable storage.

These measures may require less investment than replacing an entire production process, although their effectiveness depends on the specific facility.

Efficient Use of Water, Energy and Materials

Industries can reduce waste by improving process control, using energy-efficient equipment, recovering suitable waste heat and recirculating water where technically appropriate.

A process that produces the same amount of useful output while consuming less water has improved water-use efficiency. However, lower water consumption does not automatically establish that its remaining wastewater is safe.

Substitution of Hazardous Inputs

Where suitable alternatives exist, a factory may replace a more hazardous chemical with a less hazardous material that performs the required function. Such substitution can reduce risks to workers and the surrounding environment.

A substitute must still be assessed for its own hazards and overall performance. Replacing a chemical does not make a process automatically pollution-free.

Reuse of Suitable Process Materials

Some by-products, materials or water streams can be recovered and reused within the factory. For instance, a textile unit may recirculate suitable process water or use reclaimed water for a purpose that meets the necessary quality requirements.

Cleaner Production Versus End-of-Pipe Treatment

End-of-pipe treatment manages pollutants after they have been generated. Examples include treating industrial effluent before discharge or using pollution-control equipment to remove contaminants from exhaust gases.

FeatureCleaner productionEnd-of-pipe treatment
Principal aimPrevent or reduce waste generationRemove or control pollutants already generated
Typical actionRepair a leak or reduce excessive chemical useTreat contaminated wastewater
Point of actionWithin product or process design and operationAt or after the waste-generating stage
RoleReduces resource use and pollution at sourceControls remaining pollution and supports safe discharge

The approaches are complementary, not mutually exclusive. Cleaner production may reduce the amount of effluent, but remaining effluent still requires appropriate treatment when it contains harmful pollutants.

Gujarat Illustration: Textile Processing

Consider a textile-processing unit in an industrial area of Gujarat. The unit can improve resource efficiency by measuring chemical dosage, reducing water losses, recirculating suitable water and maintaining equipment. It must still manage its residual effluent safely.

Such a factory illustrates a general principle: a useful industrial product can be manufactured with fewer wasted inputs, but industrial activity continues to have environmental responsibilities.

Prelims focus

  • Cleaner production is preventive rather than limited to disposal or treatment.
  • RECP stands for Resource Efficient and Cleaner Production.
  • Reducing leaks and improving process control are cleaner-production measures.
  • Effluent treatment is primarily a pollution-control measure for wastewater already generated.
  • Input substitution may reduce hazards but does not automatically eliminate them.
  • Trap: Cleaner production does not remove the need to treat remaining harmful emissions or effluents.

[Sources: UNIDO, Resource Efficient and Cleaner Production, definition and resource-efficiency approach, consulted 2 November 2026; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8 Geography, Chapter 5, Industries, printed pp. 50–53; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, Chapter 12, Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems, printed pp. 135–137.]

title: Cleaner Production: Preventing Industrial Pollution at Source

body:
Meaning of Resource Efficiency

Resource efficiency means obtaining useful goods and services while avoiding unnecessary consumption or loss of materials, water, energy and other resources.

It applies to households, cities, industries and public infrastructure. A bus that carries more passengers per unit of fuel, a factory that uses less water per unit of output and a building that needs less electricity for cooling are all examples of improved efficiency under suitable conditions.

Resource efficiency should be distinguished from the simple act of using a renewable resource. A solar-powered process can still waste water or raw materials, while an energy-efficient process may still use non-renewable energy.

Resource Productivity and Resource Intensity

Two useful ways to describe efficiency are:

  • Resource productivity: the amount of useful output obtained per unit of resource consumed. Higher productivity generally indicates more output from a given resource input.
  • Resource intensity: the amount of a resource consumed per unit of useful output. Lower intensity generally indicates greater efficiency, provided the output is comparable.

For example, suppose a factory initially manufactures 100 units of a product using 1,000 litres of water. Its water intensity is 10 litres per product unit. After improvements, it uses 8 litres per product unit. Its water-use efficiency has improved.

However, if the factory then manufactures 200 units, its total water use becomes 1,600 litres. This is greater than the original total of 1,000 litres, even though water consumption per unit has decreased.

Lower resource use per unit does not necessarily mean lower total resource use. The total impact also depends on the scale of production or consumption.

Linear and Circular Use of Resources

In a conventional linear economy, resources are extracted, made into products, used and eventually discarded. A circular economy seeks to keep products and materials useful for longer, prevent unnecessary waste and recover materials when further use is no longer possible.

Common circular approaches include:

  • Reduce: avoid unnecessary material or product consumption.
  • Reuse: use an item again without first converting it into raw material.
  • Repair: restore a product so that it can continue serving its purpose.
  • Recycle: process discarded material into material suitable for further manufacturing or use.
  • Recover: obtain useful value, such as energy or material, from suitable residual waste where appropriate.

These approaches are related but not interchangeable. Washing and refilling a reusable container is reuse; processing discarded plastic into material for a new product is recycling.

Why Prevention Comes Before Recycling

Recycling can reduce demand for some virgin raw materials, but it may still require collection, sorting, transport, energy and additional processing. Some materials cannot be recycled indefinitely at the same quality, and some discarded items are unsuitable for recycling.

Consequently, avoiding unnecessary production and extending a product's useful life can sometimes conserve more resources than relying exclusively on recycling.

For a city, this may mean preventing food waste and encouraging durable goods. For an industry, it may mean improving product design, reducing production scrap or reusing suitable materials within manufacturing.

Link with Sustainable Development Goal 12

SDG 12 concerns responsible consumption and production. Two particularly relevant targets are:

  • Target 12.2: achieve sustainable management and efficient use of natural resources by 2030.
  • Target 12.5: substantially reduce waste generation through prevention, reduction, recycling and reuse by 2030.

SDG 11 principally addresses sustainable cities and communities, while SDG 12 principally addresses consumption and production patterns. Their applications overlap: a city with effective waste prevention and material recovery contributes to both aims.

Prelims focus

  • Resource productivity relates useful output to resource input.
  • Resource intensity relates resource input to useful output.
  • Reuse does not require conversion of the item back into raw material.
  • Recycling involves processing discarded material for further use.
  • SDG 12.2 concerns efficient resource use; SDG 12.5 concerns waste reduction.
  • Trap: A reduction in water or energy consumption per product unit does not guarantee a reduction in total consumption.

[Sources: UNIDO, Resource Efficient and Cleaner Production, sections on production efficiency and resource use, consulted 2 November 2026; United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Sustainable Development Goal 12, Targets 12.2 and 12.5, consulted 2 November 2026; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11 Economics, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 164–175; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 16, Environmental Issues, section 16.3, Solid Wastes.]

pictures.alt: Linear use ends in disposal; circular use extends a container's life through reuse and repair, then returns recycled material to manufacturing.
pictures.caption: A circular approach seeks to retain products and materials in useful use instead of discarding them after a single use.

title: Resource Efficiency and the Circular Economy
